text: Next, the real page. A contact form that counts and clears. Now think of the contact form of an online shop. Under the message box, a small line counts the letters as the user types, something like twelve out of two hundred. This form needs two things from its boxes. First, the count must change on every key, so the text must reach state on every key, not only when the user clicks send. Second, after send, every box must be empty again, ready for the next message. Our code empties the state, so state must be able to reach back into the box and empty it too. A box that only reports to state fails the second job. A box that only listens to state fails the first job. This lecture shows how one box does both jobs. Let's meet our example page, the Contact Us form. Our page is the Contact Us form of an online shop. It has a name box, a topic menu, a message box with its count, a tick box called Email Me a Reply, and a Send button. When the tick box is ticked, an email box appears, and this is the finished page. Figure four shows it the way it looks when the page opens. A heading, Contact Us, a name box, a topic menu already showing Delivery, then a message box and under it the count zero out of two hundred. Below that, the tick box, Email Me a Reply, still unticked, and the Send button at the bottom. The project has four files. The whole form lives in one component, Contact Form. Figure five lays those files out like a file explorer for the project contact page with the job of each file beside it. At the top is index.html, the entry. It's the HTML page with the empty root div where React mounts. Then the src folder, which holds the component modules. Main.jsx is the boundary. It imports app and mounts it inside strict mode into the root div. App.jsx is the parent. It exports app as default and renders contact form. And inside the components folder sits contactform.jsx, the default export, which holds every box and its state. The main component only places the form on the page, and you can see how little it does. In app.jsx, line one imports contact form from the components folder. Line three starts app, and line four just returns the contact form tag. The note there says React calls contact form, which holds the whole form. That's it. We start with only the message box and its count. Each principle adds one more part until the form is finished. A few ideas from earlier lessons come back here. From Lesson Twelve, useState keeps a value between renders, and calling it setter makes React render the component again. From Lesson Eleven, React hands every event handler an event object, e, and e.target is the element where the event started. Inside a handler on a box, e.target.value is the text in the box. You met that once in Lesson Seventeen. Also from Lesson Eleven, a form's submit handler calls e.preventDefault so the browser does not reload the page. And from Lesson Eighteen, a label tag around a box makes its text clickable, and a tick box keeps its own tick inside the browser.
